This example demonstrates a complete setup using Logiks Reports. It includes: API data source Table view Toolbar (search, export) Filters Actions Formatters

import { Reports } from "logiks-reports"; const reportJson = { title: "User Management", template: "table", source: { type: "API", method: "get", url: "/api/users", headers: { Authorization: "Bearer TOKEN", }, }, rowsPerPage: 10, uiswitcher: true, datagrid: { id: { label: "ID", sortable: true, }, name: { label: "Name", searchable: true, }, email: { label: "Email", searchable: true, }, status: { label: "Status", filter: { type: "select", options: { active: "Active", inactive: "Inactive", }, }, }, created_at: { label: "Created On", formatter: "date", }, }, toolbar: { search: true, export: true, print: true, }, actions: { "forms@users.create": { label: "Add User", icon: "fa fa-plus", }, }, buttons: { "forms@users.edit/{id}": { label: "Edit", icon: "fa fa-pen", }, "popup@users.view/{id}": { label: "View", icon: "fa fa-eye", }, }, }; export default function App() { return ( <Reports report={reportJson} onButtonClick={(key, row) => { console.log("Action:", key, row); }} /> ); }

Gantt view displays data as a timeline of tasks. It is useful for: Project planning Task tracking Timeline visualization
Maps your dataset fields to Gantt chart structure. "colmap": { "id": "id", "name": "task_name", "start": "start_date", "end": "end_date" }

Each record becomes a task on timeline. Example data: { "id": 1, "task_name": "Design Phase", "start_date": "2026-04-01", "end_date": "2026-04-10", "completion": 50 } 👉 Displays: Task bar from Apr 1 → Apr 10 50% progress
Use Gantt when: You have start & end dates Tasks are time-bound Dependencies matter
Project timelines Sprint planning Resource scheduling
Missing: id start end 👉 Chart may break or not render
Keep task hierarchy clean Use progress for tracking Avoid too many nested levels Use meaningful task names
Gantt is stricter than other templates Requires structured data Works best with backend-prepared data
This example shows how to create a Kanban board for managing tasks or leads. Use this when: You have status-based data You want visual workflow tracking

import { Reports } from "logiks-reports"; import "logiks-reports/index.css"; const data = [ { id: 1, name: "Lead 1", description: "Initial contact", status: "new", owner: "John", rating: 3, }, { id: 2, name: "Lead 2", description: "Follow-up pending", status: "in_progress", owner: "Jane", rating: 5, }, { id: 3, name: "Lead 3", description: "Closed deal", status: "completed", owner: "Mike", rating: 4, }, ]; const reportJson = { title: "CRM Pipeline", template: "kanban", kanban: { colkeys: { status: { label: "Status" }, }, colmap: { title: "name", descs: "description", category: "status", tags: "owner", counter: "rating", }, }, buttons: { "forms@leads.edit/{id}": { label: "Edit", icon: "fa fa-pen", }, "infoview@leads.view/{id}": { label: "View", icon: "fa fa-eye", }, }, }; export default function App() { return ( <Reports report={reportJson} data={data} onButtonClick={(key, row) => { console.log("Action:", key, row); }} /> ); }

Logiks Reports is a React library to generate dynamic reports using JSON configuration.
Remove old version first npm uninstall logiks-reports Install the required version npm install git+https://github.com/LogiksReactPlugins/LogiksReports.git#<Version>

import { Reports } from "logiks-reports"; import "logiks-reports/index.css"; //optional const reportJson = { title: "Users", datagrid: { name: { label: "Name" }, email: { label: "Email" }, }, }; export default function App() { <Reports methods={{ ...apiMethods }} report={reportJson} onButtonClick={handleAction} api={api} />; }

onButtonClick: Required This function is used to handle all button triggers and find what action to do . get (buttonKey, data) in return report: Required JSON config object that defines the report structure methods: Optional Custom methods api: Optional Holds API interface methods
style: optional Custom styling for the report

Logiks Reports allows you to define interactive actions at two levels: Actions → Global (top-level) Buttons → Row-level (per record) These are used to trigger events like: Create Edit View Navigate (Change Page, Open forms, Open Popups, etc.) API Calls

Actions appear at the top of the report (e.g., "Add New"). Example: "actions": { "forms@module_name.filename": { "label": "Add User", "icon": "fa fa-plus", "policy": "user.create.access", "class": "btn btn-info", "onselect": true, "lgksConfirm": "Are you sure?", "lgksPrompt": "Are you sure?", "lgksAlert": "Are you sure?", } }

Property Description label Action label, can also include dynamic content icon Action icon, supports Font awesome policy Access policy class CSS class, supports custom and tailwind classes onselect When true: shows the action button on click else shows the action button always lgksConfirm Confirm message lgksPrompt Prompt message, capable od taking user input lgksAlert Alert message Key definition for object actions: Key definition for object actions, where the object key can be method name like handleCreateAction, or entity@module_name.filename, Methods are simple functions that will be called when the action is triggered. Where as entity is a type of action that can be triggered like page, popup, forms, popup.forms, infoview, popup.infoview, report, popup.report, api

Key format: "type@module_name.filename" Example: forms@vendor.new → open form for new record from sliding from left popup.forms@vendor.new → opens popup with form for new record api@vendor.delete → calls the routes defined in module vendor at routes.js file, here vendor is the module name and delete is the route defined in routes.js.

Use actions when: You want a global button Action is NOT tied to a specific row, but when a row is selected and the action button is clicked then that rows object will be passed and if multiple rows are selected then an array of objects will be passed. Examples: Add new record Bulk operations

Buttons are displayed for each row in the report. Example: "buttons": { "infoview@test": { "label": "View", "icon": "fa fa-eye" }, "forms@edit": { "label": "Edit", "icon": "fa fa-pen" } } Note: Buttons also shares same object as actions excepts for onselect, only difference is that it is for row-level actions.
Use buttons when: Action depends on row data You need row-specific operations

The labels appears as tools tips on the icons, the same labels appears as Title on the popups. If there number of button are more that 5 then a 3 dot icon appears, and other button options are displayed in the context menu which shows the labels. Example 1: Static label "page@eoffice.chat": { "label": "Add Vendor Form", "icon": "fa-solid fa-circle-info" } Example 2: Dynamic label "page@eoffice.chat": { "label": "{file_code}", "icon": "fa-solid fa-circle-info" } Example 3: Custom label "page@eoffice.chat": { "label": "{file_code} - Add form", "icon": "fa-solid fa-circle-info" }

When API is used on actions The entire actions object is passed to the API. If a single row is selects then that row's id is passed in ids:[]. If multiple rows are selected then an array of ids will be passed along with the action object. API support queryString for action You can use queryString in the API URL, the queryString will be appended to the URL. It has the feature to pass the dynamic values from the rows. Example: "api@eoffice.chat?key1=value1&key2={file_code}": { "label": "{file_code} - Add form", "icon": "fa-solid fa-circle-info" } When API is used on buttons The entire row object along with the button object are passed to the API. API support queryString for buttons You can use queryString in the API URL, the queryString will be appended to the URL. A fixed value can be passed in the queryString. Example: "api@eoffice.chat?key1=value1": { "label": "{file_code} - Add form", "icon": "fa-solid fa-circle-info" }
This section now answers: What are actions vs buttons When to use each How to handle clicks Real examples Common mistakes
Defines how data is displayed in calendar view. Note: The datagrid object is required along with calendar, as calendar events are derived from the data columns defined in the datagrid.
Maps data columns from the datagrid to calendar event fields. Each key represents a predefined calendar event component, and the value should match a column key from the datagrid. Supported mappings:
Primary title shown for the calendar event. Example: "title": "persona_name"
Description or additional details shown for the event. Example: "descs": "persona_desc"

Defines which date columns should be rendered as calendar events. Each key should reference a date column from the datagrid, and its value defines the event color. Example: "date_col": { "created_on": "#9428C8", "edited_on": "#3653C6" } In this example: created_on events appear with color #9428C8 edited_on events appear with color #3653C6
This allows multiple date fields from the same record to appear as separate event types in the calendar. Common examples: Created Date Due Date Updated Date Deadline Follow-up Date
Defines the route or UI link opened when a calendar event is clicked. Example: "unilink": "staff.main" This opens the linked UI destination when the event is selected.

Displays custom HTML notes, legends, or event indicators in the calendar UI. Example: "notes_user": "
created onedited on
" Typical uses: Color legends Event type indicators User instructions Custom notes Supports custom HTML.

calendar uses values from the datagrid dataset and does not define independent data. colmap controls event content. date_col defines which date columns appear on the calendar. Multiple date fields can be displayed simultaneously. unilink is optional and enables event navigation. notes_user is optional and is commonly used for legends or helper notes.

Defines how data is displayed in card view. Note: The datagrid object is required along with cards, as card fields are derived from the data columns defined in the datagrid. Example: "cards": { "colmap": { "title": "persona_name", "descs": "persona_descs", "category": "type", "due_date": "created_on", "avatar": "persona_avatar", "color": "status" }, "colormap": { "active": "card_green", "under_notice": "card_red", "probationary": "card_blue" }, "unilink": "staff.main", "default_avatar": true }
Maps data columns from the datagrid to card UI elements. Each key represents a predefined card component, and the value should match a column key from the datagrid. Supported mappings:
Primary heading of the card. Example: "title": "persona_name" Displays the value from the persona_name column as the card title.
Description or summary text displayed in the card body. Example: "descs": "persona_descs"
Displays a category, type, or label for the card. Example: "category": "type"
Displays date-related information on the card. Example: "due_date": "created_on"
Defines the column used to display an avatar or profile image. Example: "avatar": "persona_avatar"
Defines which data column controls card color mapping using colormap. Example: "color": "status" If status is active, the corresponding color class from colormap will be applied.

Maps column values (usually from the field defined in colmap.color) to CSS classes for card styling. Example: "colormap": { "active": "card_green", "under_notice": "card_red", "probationary": "card_blue" } In this example: active → applies card_green under_notice → applies card_red probationary → applies card_blue Useful for status-based card colors.
Defines the route or UI link used when clicking a card. Example: "unilink": "staff.main" This opens the linked UI destination when the card is selected.
Displays a default avatar when no avatar value is available. Example: "default_avatar": true true → fallback avatar shown when image is missing false → no fallback avatar

cards uses values from the datagrid dataset and does not define independent data. colmap values must reference valid keys in the datagrid. colormap is optional and used only for value-based color styling. default_avatar is optional. unilink is optional and used for card navigation.
Defines how data fields are displayed.
The key of the object in the datagrid represents the column name of the data.
Column name, which is visible in the UI as the header.

It may happen that the source data contains multiple columns which are not required to be displayed in the report but user can have the option to view them as need basis. So hidden allows to hide those columns, but the hidden columns can be enabled from settings.
Enable search of the column, it will appear in the search bar under the select drowdown, where user can select the column name to search the text.
Enable sorting for the column, sorting is done by clicking the column header. The column can be sorted in ascending or descending order.

It opens a dropdown with the list of columns where groupable is set to true. Enable grouping for the data, if the report support grid view then the grid will be grouped by the rows. If the report support kanban view then the kanban will be grouped by the columns. For other reports the groupable feature will be hidden
Enable grouping for the column, all the columns with the same group will be grouped together. You can use this to group columns by category.

The column data can be formatted using the formatter property. Example url is used to display a link, which can be clicked to open the link in a new tab. You can refer to Formatters for more information.
Custom CSS classes or tailwind classes

The filter gets activated as inline filter for grid view only. The inline filter above each columns can have various elements/components which is defined by type property of the filter. If the type holds daterange which is special case, then the inline filter will not be activated for those columns, rather a separate Date Range filter will be activated on top of the reports. If multiple columns contains daterange then the a dropdown filter will be shown to first select the column to apply date range filter. Example 1: Adds a dropdown filter, where options are defined in the options object Type can be of following values.
allows text search for the columns Example: "filter": { "type": "text" }
allows date search for the columns. The accepted format is YYYY-MM-DD which is default set in calendar. Example: "filter": { "type": "date" }
allows month search for the columns from the Calendar Example: "filter": { "type":"month" }
allows date range search for the columns which is added at the top of the report Example: "filter": { "type": "daterange" }
allows select search for the columns

Example: Dynamic value from JSON SQL query. "filter": { "type": "dataSelectorFromUniques", "table": "data_qc_frequency_master_tbl", "columns": "created_by,created_by" } This object structure is similar to source object. Refer to source for more information. Example: Fixed value "filter": { "type": "select", "options": { "active": "Active" } }
Defines how data is displayed in gallery view. Note: The datagrid object is required along with gallery, as gallery items are derived from the data columns defined in the datagrid.
Maps data columns from the datagrid to gallery item UI elements. Each key represents a predefined gallery component, and the value should match a column key from the datagrid. Supported mappings:
Defines the image, thumbnail, or media displayed for the gallery item. Example: "avatar": "persona_avatar" Typically used for: Images Profile photos Product thumbnails Media previews
Primary heading of the gallery item. Example: "title": "persona_name" Displayed as the main label or title.
Description or summary text shown for the gallery item. Example: "descs": "persona_desc" Used for supporting information or captions.
Displays secondary metadata such as date, code, or identifier. Example: "due_date": "persona_code" Common uses: Codes or IDs Dates Reference values Additional labels

gallery uses values from the datagrid dataset and does not define independent data. colmap controls how each gallery item is rendered. All colmap values must reference valid keys in the datagrid. avatar is typically the primary visual element in gallery view. Additional mappings can be extended as supported by the UI renderer.
Defines how data is displayed in Gantt chart view. Note: The datagrid object is required along with gantt, as Gantt task data is derived from the data columns defined in the datagrid.
Maps data columns from the datagrid to Gantt chart task fields. Each key represents a predefined Gantt component, and the value should match a column key from the datagrid. Supported mappings:
Unique identifier for the task. Example: "id": "id" Used internally to identify each task.
Task name displayed in the Gantt chart. Example: "name": "persona_name" Shown as the task label.
Defines the task start date. Example: "start": "created_on" Must reference a valid date field.
Defines the task end date. Example: "end": "end_date" Used with start to determine task duration.
Defines task completion progress. Example: "progress": "completion" Commonly represented as a percentage. Example values: 25 50 100
Defines the task owner or assignee. Example: "owner": "assigned_to" Can be used to show responsibility or resource ownership.
Marks whether a task is a milestone. Example: "milestone": "is_milestone" Typical values: true false Milestones may render differently than standard tasks.
Defines parent-child hierarchy for nested tasks. Example: "parent": "parent_id" Used for grouping subtasks under a parent task.
Defines task dependencies. Example: "dependencies": "depends_on" Used to link tasks based on predecessor relationships. Examples: Single dependency Multiple dependencies Dependency chains

gantt uses values from the datagrid dataset and does not define independent data. colmap controls how tasks are rendered in the Gantt chart. All colmap values must reference valid keys in the datagrid. id, name, start, and end are typically required. parent enables hierarchical task grouping. dependencies enables linked task scheduling. milestone and progress are optional but commonly used.

Defines how data is displayed in map view using geolocation markers. Note: The datagrid object is required along with gmap, as map markers and details are derived from the data columns defined in the datagrid.
Defines the default map zoom level. Example: "zoom": 4 Higher values zoom in closer. Typical examples: 2 → World view 4 → Region / country view 10 → City view 15+ → Street level
Defines the map display type or style. Example: "mapid": "terrain" Possible examples may include: terrain roadmap satellite hybrid Supported values depend on the map renderer.
Maps data columns from the datagrid to map marker data. Each key represents a predefined map component, and the value should match a column key from the datagrid. Supported mappings:
Primary title shown for the map marker or popup. "title": "name"
Description or supporting details shown in marker info. "descs": "info"

Defines the column containing geographic coordinates. "geolocation": "geo" Used to place markers on the map. Expected data may include: Latitude / Longitude pairs Coordinates object Supported geo format required by the renderer Example: "geo": "19.9975,73.7898"

Defines a custom HTML template used for marker popups or info windows. Example:

$title

$descs

Supports placeholder variables mapped from colmap. Example placeholders: $title $descs Typical uses: Custom info windows Rich popup layouts Styled marker details

gmap uses values from the datagrid dataset and does not define independent data. colmap controls map marker content. geolocation is required for plotting markers. template is optional and allows custom popup rendering. zoom and mapid control initial map behavior. All colmap values must reference valid keys in the datagrid.
Defines how data is displayed in Kanban board view. Note: The datagrid object is required along with kanban, as Kanban fields are derived from the data columns defined in the datagrid.
Defines the Kanban columns (board lanes). Each key in colkeys represents a column available in the Kanban board. Example: "colkeys": { "status": { "label": "Status" } }
The key of the object in colkeys represents the Kanban column identifier. Example: "persona_group"
Display label shown as the Kanban column header. Example: "label": "Persona Group"
Maps data columns from the datagrid to Kanban card UI elements. Each key represents a predefined Kanban card component, and the value should match a column key from the datagrid. Supported mappings:
Primary heading of the Kanban card. "title": "persona_name"
Displays department, owner, or assigned user. "department": "created_by"
Description or summary text shown in the card body. "descs": "persona_descs"
Displays due date or date-related information. "due_date": "dtoe"
Defines the column used for avatar or profile image. "avatar": "persona_avatar"
Defines which column controls Kanban card color styling. "color": "type" Can be used for type-based visual indicators.
Displays tags or badges associated with the card. "tags": "role" Supports displaying one or multiple labels.
Displays a numeric value, count, rating, or indicator. "counter": "rating" Example uses: Task count Priority score Rating Item totals

kanban uses values from the datagrid dataset and does not define independent data. colkeys defines the Kanban lanes. colmap controls how each Kanban card is rendered. All colmap values must reference valid keys in the datagrid. Additional mappings can be extended as supported by the UI renderer.
# Local Overrides Reports can store user-specific settings like: - Column visibility - Filters - Sorting ## Behavior - Stored locally (browser) - Applied automatically on reload

Used to change the layout of the report which was defined in the pages via slot-binding. These slots are already been used in the pages which are defined in the layout. Refer to [slot-binding](/module-guide/references/slot-bindings)
Reset the toolbar by setting the value to empty string. This is used to reset the toolbar. Example: "slotBindings": { "app-toolbar.toolbar": "" }
Specify the name of the component to inject. Example "slotBindings": { "app-toolbar.toolbar": "side-bar" }
Specify multiple name of the component to reset/inject in arrayx. Example "slotBindings": { "app-toolbar.toolbar": ["side-bar"] }

Used to apply conditional styling to rows or columns. Example for adding style to a row "rules": { "row_class": { "allow_staff_update": { "yes": "allow_update_staff", "no": "not_allow_update_staff" } } }

When you want to highlight a row based on a condition, for example, if the "allow_staff_update" field is "yes", you can apply the "allow_update_staff" class to that row, and if it's "no", you can apply the "not_allow_update_staff" class. This can be useful for visually distinguishing rows that meet certain criteria, such as highlighting rows where staff updates are allowed or not allowed. Example for adding style to a column "rules": { "col_class": { "allow_staff_update": { "yes": "allow_update_staff", "no": "not_allow_update_staff" } } }

When you want to highlight a column based on a condition, for example, if the "allow_staff_update" field is "yes", you can apply the "allow_update_staff" class to that column, and if it's "no", you can apply the "not_allow_update_staff" class. This can be useful for visually distinguishing columns that meet certain criteria, such as highlighting columns where staff updates are allowed or not allowed. In both cases, you would need to define the CSS classes "allow_update_staff" and "not_allow_update_staff" in your stylesheet to specify the desired styling for those conditions. Note: The actual implementation of how these rules are applied may depend on the specific reporting tool or framework you are using, so make sure to refer to the documentation of that tool for any additional configuration or syntax requirements.

Source is property of Reports that allows to fetch the data using API, methods or executing SQL query (SQL query is supported by JSON object). When the SQL JSON Object is passed, then the application replace it with query id and the report library calls the API to get the response.
The source is responsible to fetch the data for the Reports. There are 3 types of sources from which data can be fetched.

An JSON Object support SQL query which is used to fetch the data. The developer pass the JSON Object to the Report to fetch the data. The Report internally executes the query and return the data to the Report. A sql example using System Variables, multiple joins and nested sql query. Example: "source": { "type": "sql", "table": "data_camp_location", "cols": "data_camp_location.*, company_tbl.title, data_sector.title, data_project_function.title", "cols_count": "count(distinct eoffice_files_tbl.id) as count", "join": [ { "type": "left", "query": "company_tbl", "condition": "data_camp_location.company_code_id = company_tbl.id" }, { "type": "left", "query": "data_sector", "condition": "data_camp_location.sector_id = data_sector.id" }, { "type": "left", "query": "data_project_function", "condition": "data_camp_location.project_id = data_project_function.id" }, { "type": "INNER", "query": "data_datahub_matrix", "condition": "FIND_IN_SET(data_camp_location.project_id, data_datahub_matrix.project_function_ids)" } ], "where": { "data_camp_location.blocked": "false", "data_datahub_matrix.userid": "#SESS_USER_ID#" }, "orderby": "data_camp_location.id desc", "groupby": "data_camp_location.id", "limit": 1000 } Please check below link for other options and example for SQL Sample Examples​
Here the data is fetched using a method. The method gets triggered when the Report is loaded. "source": { "type": "method", "method": "handleCreateAction" }

The data can be loaded directly from the external API. "source": { "type": "API", "method": "post", "url": "https://ai.smartinfologiks.com/api/users", "params": { "name": "John Doe", "email": "8K0oJ@example.com" } "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN", }, }

The toolbar provides quick access to common actions like: Search Print Email Export: Supported format "pdf", "csv", "xml", "htm", "img" Export All You can enable or disable these features using the toolbar configuration. Example: "toolbar": { "search": true, "print": true, "email": false, "export": ["pdf", "csv"] || true, "exportAll": true }

"search": true What it does Adds a search input to filter report data. When to use When users need quick filtering Works best with datagrid.searchable, the searchable fields shows the columns that can be searched. To add the column in the dropdown add a properties field with searchable: true in the datagrid array of object configuration. Example: "datagrid": { "name": { "label": "Name", "searchable": true } } Important Notes Search will not be effective, if no columns are marked as searchable "searchable": false
"print": true What it does​ Allows users to print the report. When to use​ Reports shared offline Admin dashboards Important Notes Large tables may not print cleanly Consider limiting columns
"email": true What it does Provides option to email report data. When to use Reporting workflows Sharing reports with stakeholders

"export": ["csv", "excel"] What it does Allows exporting report data. Supported formats csv excel xml htm img pdf (if supported) export vs exportAll export → exports current view exportAll → exports full dataset When to use Data analysis Reporting External usage Options export → current view exportAll → full dataset ** Important Notes ** Ensure data is available API should return proper structure
Enable only required options Avoid cluttering toolbar Use search + filter together Enable export for reports, not dashboards
Enabling search without searchable fields Enabling all options unnecessarily - Leads to cluttered UI Empty export array Empty exportAll array
Formatters control how data is displayed and core formatter engine
(⚠️ mark as “details needs to be added for each formatter with example”)

Calendar view displays your data as events based on date fields. It is useful when your dataset contains time-based information such as: Created date Due date Updated date
Maps data fields to calendar event content. "colmap": { "title": "name", "descs": "description" }
title (Required)​ Main event title descs​ Additional description shown in event
Maps date fields to event colors Each date field creates events on calendar
If your data contains: { "name": "Task A", "created_on": "2026-04-01", "edited_on": "2026-04-03" } 👉 It will create: Event on April 1 (created_on) Event on April 3 (edited_on)
You can track multiple events per record: "date_col": { "created_on": "#333", "due_date": "red", "completed_on": "green" }
Allows custom HTML (e.g., legend) Useful to explain colors
Use Calendar when: Data is date-driven You need timeline visualization Tracking events over time
Task deadlines Activity logs Event scheduling
Without it: 👉 No events will appear
Use clear color coding Limit number of date fields (2–3) Provide legend using notes_user Use meaningful titles

Gantt view displays data as a timeline of tasks. It is useful for: Project planning Task tracking Timeline visualization
Maps your dataset fields to Gantt chart structure. "colmap": { "id": "id", "name": "task_name", "start": "start_date", "end": "end_date" }

Each record becomes a task on timeline. Example data: { "id": 1, "task_name": "Design Phase", "start_date": "2026-04-01", "end_date": "2026-04-10", "completion": 50 } 👉 Displays: Task bar from Apr 1 → Apr 10 50% progress
Use Gantt when: You have start & end dates Tasks are time-bound Dependencies matter
Project timelines Sprint planning Resource scheduling
Missing: id start end 👉 Chart may break or not render
Keep task hierarchy clean Use progress for tracking Avoid too many nested levels Use meaningful task names
Gantt is stricter than other templates Requires structured data Works best with backend-prepared data
GMap view displays data on a geographical map using latitude and longitude. It is useful for: Location-based data Tracking assets/users Visualizing geographic distribution
Maps dataset fields to map markers. "colmap": { "title": "name", "descs": "description", "geolocation": "location" }
Your data should contain: "location": { "lat": 19.0760, "lng": 72.8777 } 👉 or string format (if supported): "location": "19.0760,72.8777"
Custom HTML for marker popup Supports variables: $title $descs
Use Map when: You have location data You want spatial visualization Tracking movement or distribution
Delivery tracking Store locations Field workforce tracking
Cluster markers for large data (if supported) Use meaningful titles Keep popup content minimal Set appropriate zoom level

Kanban view displays data in columns (like a task board), grouped by a specific field. Each column represents a category (e.g., status, stage, department).
Creates columns like: Pending In Progress Completed
Workflow tracking Task management CRM pipelines
Maps your data fields to the Kanban card UI. "colmap": { "title": "name", "descs": "description", "category": "status" }
"category": "status" Determines which column the card goes into
Use Kanban when: You need workflow tracking Data has stages/status Visual grouping is required
Task management board Lead pipeline (New → Contacted → Closed) Approval workflows
If your data doesn't include: status name 👉 Cards will not render properly
